newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean tycoon admits giving money to Kim's aide.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean tycoon admits giving money to Kim's aide.

text.p: The founder of South Korea's controversial Hanbo Group said on Monday he had helped finance election campaigns for a close political associate of President Kim Young-sam but denied bribing him.

Chung Tae-soo told a Seoul criminal court that he had sent his company executive to Mayor Moon Jung-soo of Pusan, South Korea's second largest city, to deliver 200 million won ($225,000). "The 200 million won handed over to Mayor Moon...was election funds," Chung said, adding the money was given before Moon was elected mayor in 1995.

Moon and seven serving or former lawmakers are on trial on charges of taking bribes from Chung, who is again on trial for corruption after being jailed last month for 15 years in a loans-for-kickbacks scandal.

The scandal also landed three other close associates of the president -- one a former cabinet minister -- in jail along with bankers and businessmen. Moon, a member of Kim's inner circle that played a leading role in his 1992 election victory, has pleaded not guilty to bribery charges.
Moon told the court that he had not received any money from Chung, reversing his testimony during an investigaton by state prosecutors.

"I told prosecutors that my brother had accepted 100 million won from Hanbo because I wanted to reduce the size of the money and avoid being prosecuted amid suspicions that I had taken 200 million won," he said.
"In view of past practices that one would not be punished for accepting political funds, I thought a solution was likely. But in fact I have not received money," he added.

State prosecutors accused Moon and the other politicians of taking kickbacks from the founder of Hanbo, whose steel-making flagship collapsed in January under five trillion won of debts, revealing a web of corruption. All other defendants pleaded not guilty to bribery charges.
Fierce public criticism over the Hanbo scandal and opposition allegations that President Kim's second son, Kim Hyun-chul, was behind the controversy dealt a dire blow to Kim's presidency.

The prosecution has cleared Kim Hyun-chul of any involvement in the loans-for-kickbacks scandal, but arrested him on charges of bribery in unrelated cases and on tax evasion. He is due to go on trial next week.
Opposition parties have accused Chung of helping bankroll the president's 1992 election victory and that Kim Hyun-chul laundered huge sums of leftover funds through business cronies.

The main opposition National Congress for New Politics on Monday alleged that President Kim spent more than 1.3 trillion won for his election, against the legally set maximum spending of 36.7 billion won.
Kim's ruling New Korea Party had earlier reported that the amount spent was 28.4 billion won. But some party members have privately admitted that the actual campaign financing far exceeded the sum.

Kim Young-sam last month apologised for spending a large sum on his election campaign but refused to yield to opposition demands that he reveal details of the financing. The trial of the politicians was adjourned until July 14. (Conversion: $ = 888 won)
